analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits and funds them with payroll taxes on income above $250,000 plus higher investment taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after its February 2019 introduction it sat in three House committees for the remaining two years of the Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise Social Security benefits for all beneficiaries — eventually by 15% — recalculate annual cost-of-living increases using an index that tracks what seniors actually spend, guarantee a minimum benefit at the poverty line for people who worked long careers at low wages, and let students of retired, deceased, or disabled workers stay on benefits until age 22. To pay for it and extend the program's solvency, it would apply the Social Security payroll tax to wages and self-employment income above $250,000 a year (today earnings above roughly $133,000 are exempt) and raise the tax on high-income investment gains from 3.8% to 10%. It would also merge the retirement and disability trust funds into one Social Security Trust Fund.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries. Every beneficiary would get an across-the-board raise phasing in to 15% by 2039 [S3]. Cost-of-living adjustments would switch to the CPI-E, an index built on the spending of older households, which typically rises faster than the index used now [S3]. Retirees and disabled workers who spent decades in low-wage work would get a new minimum benefit tied to the federal poverty guideline — reaching 125% of poverty for those with 30 or more years of work [S3]. Children of retired, deceased, or disabled workers could collect benefits as full-time students until 22 instead of aging out at 19 [S3]. And the added tax revenue would extend the program's solvency, protecting benefits for future retirees [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees, disabled workers, and low-wage seniors

how_it_helps.text: Raises every Social Security benefit with an across-the-board increase of 1 percentage point a year starting in 2025, reaching 15% in 2039 and staying there.

Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which measures the basket of goods older Americans actually buy, such as health care and housing, rather than the general urban index used now.

Creates a new minimum benefit for lifetime low earners: after 10 years of work the benefit climbs with each additional year, reaching 125% of the federal poverty guideline for someone with 30 or more years of work, so a full career at low wages no longer leaves a retiree in poverty.
Lets children of retired, deceased, or disabled workers receive benefits until age 22 as full-time students, instead of losing them at 19.

Pays for the expansion and extends solvency by applying the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax to wages and self-employment income above $250,000 — under current law 2019 earnings above $132,900 were exempt — and by raising the net investment income tax on high earners from 3.8% to 10%.
Merges the retirement and disability trust funds into a single Social Security Trust Fund, ending the annual ritual in which one fund is projected to run short while the other has a surplus.

analysis.who_pays: High-income households. People with wages or self-employment income above $250,000 a year would pay the 12.4% Social Security tax on everything above that line, which today escapes the tax entirely [S2][S3]. Households with high investment income would pay 10% instead of 3.8% on their net investment gains — a 6.2-point increase aimed at income that now largely avoids Social Security taxes [S3].

drawbacks.text: The tax increase is steep and falls entirely at the top: a household earning above $250,000 would pay the full 12.4% payroll tax on every dollar past that line, and investment income would jump from a 3.8% to a 10% levy — a real cost that critics would call a large tax hike on savers and job creators.

The bill has a design quirk: earnings between the current taxable maximum (about $133,000) and $250,000 would remain untaxed, creating a gap where the payroll tax disappears and then reappears — an uneven structure that tax analysts would flag.
The benefit increase is slow to arrive: the across-the-board raise starts in 2025 at 1% and does not reach the full 15% until 2039, so today's beneficiaries would wait years for the full boost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and concrete — a 15% raise, poverty-level minimums for lifetime low earners, faster COLAs, and extended solvency for a program roughly 60 million-plus Americans rely on. The costs fall on a narrow, high-income group: earners above $250,000 and households with large investment income. An honest supporter would concede the top-end tax increase is large and the bill's gap between the current wage cap and $250,000 is an awkward design; an honest opponent would have to concede the money goes to extend and expand a program that broadly benefits working people, not to a new entitlement for the wealthy.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the Social Security Expansion Act on February 13, 2019, and it was referred that day to the Ways and Means Committee plus the Education and Labor and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees.
Within two days it was further referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security and a Transportation subcommittee — the standard path for a bill a committee does not plan to move.
No hearing, mark-up, committee vote, or floor action ever followed. The bill sat in committee until the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and died there.
It attracted 26 cosponsors, all of them Democrats out of 231 House Democrats, and no Republicans; that level of support was not enough to get committee leadership to schedule it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners and wealthy investors are better off because the bill died: the payroll-tax cap above which their earnings escape Social Security tax stays in place, and the net investment income tax remains 3.8% instead of rising to 10%.

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors for a benefit expansion funded by taxes on income above $250,000 and higher investment taxes.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee with jurisdiction over Social Security referred the bill to its Social Security Subcommittee and never brought it to a hearing or mark-up for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; no roll-call was ever held, so the partisan split is visible only in sponsorship and the bill's silence in a Democratic-led committee.

industries.note: The bill's funding comes entirely from this group: a 12.4% payroll tax on earnings above $250,000 that currently escapes Social Security tax, and a rise in the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 10%. Its gain — keeping the cap and the lower rate — is the public's cost, since the revenue would fund benefit increases and solvency.

The bill subjects investment gain to a 10% tax, up from 3.8%, raising the tax burden on carried interest, portfolio returns, and other investment income managed by the financial sector. No industry in the bill gains; the only concentrated interests touched are those paying in.
